sceneHappening: Jesus as high priest, called by God, in the order of Melchizedek; a rebuke for being slow to learn
summary: "For every high priest, being taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God, that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. The high priest can deal gently with those who are ignorant and going astray, because he himself is also surrounded with weakness. Because of this, he must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself. Nobody takes this honor on himself, but he is called by God, just like Aaron was. So also Christ didn't glorify himself to be made a high priest, but it was he who said to him, 'You are my Son. Today I have become your father.' As he says also in another place, 'You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.'" "He, in the days of his flesh, having offered up prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard for his godly fear, though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered. Having been made perfect, he became to all of those who obey him the author of eternal salvation, named by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek." Then a rebuke: "About him we have many words to say, and hard to interpret, seeing you have become dull of hearing. For although by this time you should be teachers, you again need to have someone teach you the rudiments of the first principles of the revelations of God. You have come to need milk, and not solid food. For everyone who lives on milk is not experienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby. But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil."
whySettingMatters: The high priest was the central religious figure for Jewish readers, the one person who entered the Holy of Holies on the Day of Atonement. The chapter lists two qualifications (sympathy with the people and a divine call) and shows that Jesus has both. His sympathy is stressed in 5:7-8, which most scholars connect with Gethsemane: "prayers and petitions with strong crying and tears." That Jesus "learned obedience" and was "made perfect" does not mean he was ever disobedient; the letter has just said he was "without sin" (4:15). It means he went through the whole path of obedience to its end. The "order of Melchizedek" (Psalm 110:4) is introduced here and will be developed in chapter 7. Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18-20) was a king-priest outside the line of Aaron, so Jesus does not need Levitical descent. At 5:11 the author turns to rebuke, a blunt change of tone: the readers should be "teachers" but need "milk." "Milk" and "solid food" are common images for beginning and mature teaching (1 Corinthians 3:2). The readers are not unintelligent; they are "dull of hearing," slow to listen. The letter is about to offer demanding material in chapters 7 to 10, and the rebuke prepares them to pay attention.

Called by God as high priest; learned obedience through suffering.
The model of a priest called by God.
Introduced as the order of Jesus' priesthood.

questions: A high priest must deal "gently" because he too is weak. Why would the writer put sympathy first?
"Though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered." What does it mean that Jesus learned?
The writer says the readers should be teachers by now. What keeps believers from growing?
Milk and solid food: how do you tell if you are being nourished or just kept comfortable?

"You are my Son" (5:5) and "though he was a Son" (5:8).
"And petitions" (5:7). The word appears only here.
"Having been heard for his godly fear" (5:7).
"The author of eternal salvation" (5:9). The word means source or cause.
"To all of those who obey him" (5:9).
"Named by God a high priest" (5:10). The word appears only here.
"Hard to interpret" (5:11). The word appears only here.
"Of the revelations of God" (5:12). The Greek is "oracles."
"Is not experienced" (5:13). The word appears only here.
"By reason of use" (5:14). The word means habit.
"Their senses exercised" (5:14). The word appears only here.
